stories.headline: Election Commission caps Form 7 applications to prevent bulk voter deletions
stories.title: Election Commission caps Form 7 applications to prevent bulk voter deletions
stories.summary: The new rules require electoral registration officers to verify objections, hear applicants and give affected voters an opportunity to respond before deletion.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: To prevent bulk or malicious attempts to remove legitimate voters from electoral rolls, the Election Commission on Friday introduced specific caps on how many Form 7 applications a single registered elector can submit.
These restrictions apply equally, whether the forms are submitted online or offline.
During the special period designated for filing claims and objections – typically known as the Summary Revision period – an individual voter is allowed to submit a maximum of 10 Form 7 applications.
Once this revision period concludes, the process shifts to continuous updation.
During this routine period of voter list updation, individual voters are limited to submitting no more than five Form 7 applications in a single calendar month.
Amid reports of bulk filing of such applications or Form 7 from Karnataka and Odisha, the EC has directed all chief electoral officers to brief their field staff about the new directions.
The move aims to discourage bulk filing of unsubstantiated objections, reduce inconvenience to voters and ease the workload of election officials.

According to the reworked mechanism, the electoral registration officer (ERO) will first issue a notice to the objector, hear him personally, record his statements separately for each Form 7 and satisfy himself about the validity of the objections.
When the ERO is satisfied, he will dispose of the application as per Rules 19 and 20 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, giving an opportunity of hearing to the person objected to.
The directive seeks to curb excessive or potentially fabricated objections to electoral rolls while reinforcing verification and procedural safeguards before names are deleted.

The Commission has directed the chief electoral officers of all states and Union Territories to circulate the instructions among the EROs, assistant EROs and field-level officials and ensure adequate publicity.
What is Form 7 and who can file it?

stories.headline: Indian origin jurist Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
stories.title: Indian origin jurist Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
stories.summary: Oslo, Oct 9: South African jurist of Indian origin Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, a former UN human rights chief whose work helped shape international law on genocide and sexual violence, won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The 85-year-old jurist, who grew up under apartheid and went on to hold senior positions in South Africa’s judiciary and international legal institutions, dedicated the award to survivors of international crimes and those defending international justice, saying their “compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign”. “We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” Pillay said, pointing in particular to attacks on the International Criminal Court (ICC). One of her most recent roles was chairing the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. In September 2025, the commission concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed and were continuing to commit genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. The commission also concluded that Israeli President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then Defence Minister Yoav Gallant had incited genocide. Israel rejected the findings. The conclusions were those of an investigative body, not a final ruling by an international court. In separate remarks following the Nobel announcement, Pillay referred to the Gaza report as her most recent work, saying it had named what was happening there as genocide. Pillay is also serving as a judge in a case at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in which The Gambia has accused Myanmar of violating the Genocide Convention. She was selected by The Gambia to sit in the proceedings. Pillay learnt of the Nobel award while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, where Nazi leaders were tried after World War II. She said it was fitting that the announcement came while she was in Courtroom 600, where the trials were held. Warning that efforts to weaken international criminal justice threatened to undo progress made since the Nuremberg trials, the jurist said on Friday: “They risk returning us to a world in which power rather than law determines whose suffering matters.” In a message to political leaders, Pillay said they had a legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war. “My message to leaders, political leaders, is that you are under legal obligation,” she said. “No matter what other obligation you have morally, you have a legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war.” She urged countries to uphold the principles of the UN Charter and their obligations under international law, adding: “That is an obligation I call upon every state to fulfill.” Born in Durban on September 23, 1941, to Indian parents of Tamil descent, Pillay grew up in a poor family under apartheid. According to a biographical profile published by the Institute for African Women in Law, her father was a bus driver who worked multiple jobs to support the family, while her mother looked after their eight children. Despite financial hardship, her parents placed a strong emphasis on education and insisted that their daughters, like their sons, should be educated. Pillay studied at the University of Natal, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1963 and a law degree in 1965. She later earned postgraduate law degrees at Harvard University, including a doctorate in juridical science in 1988. In 1967, she became the first woman of colour to establish a law practice in South Africa’s Natal Province, according to the Institute for African Women in Law. She spent decades defending anti-apartheid activists and political detainees, including leaders such as Nelson Mandela, and drawing attention to torture and solitary confinement. In 1973, she helped secure political prisoners’ right to legal counsel, according to South African History Online. Her work also exposed the racial barriers within South Africa’s legal system. A Harvard Law School profile noted that, as a lawyer, she had not been allowed to enter a judge’s chambers. Pillay was involved in efforts to enshrine equality in South Africa’s Constitution. As a member of the Women’s National Coalition, she contributed to a campaign that helped secure a constitutional equality clause prohibiting discrimination. In an interview with South African History Online, she described how women from different political, racial and religious backgrounds worked together to advance equality and protect women’s rights. In 1995, a year after South Africa’s first democratic elections, Pillay became the first woman of colour to serve as an acting judge on the country’s High Court. That same year, she was elected to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, established to prosecute those responsible for genocide and other serious crimes committed during the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. She served as a judge until 2003 and was the tribunal’s president from 1999 to 2003. One of the most consequential chapters of her judicial career was her work as one of the judges in the tribunal’s landmark case against Jean-Paul Akayesu, the former mayor of Taba commune, who was convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and direct and public incitement to commit genocide. The tribunal’s 1998 judgment recognised that rape and sexual violence could constitute acts of genocide when committed with the specific intent required under the Genocide Convention. It also recognised rape as a crime against humanity in the circumstances established in the case. Akayesu’s conviction for direct and public incitement to commit genocide also established an important precedent in international criminal law. The Norwegian Nobel Committee credited Pillay with playing a significant role in the legal development concerning sexual violence. Speaking after the Nobel announcement, Pillay said she was proud that the tribunal had recognised sexual violence as an international crime. She described it as “outrageous” that sexual violence against women and children in conflict had been treated as “collateral damage or as reward for the hard fighting soldiers”. Pillay subsequently served as a judge at the International Criminal Court from 2003 to 2008, including on its Appeals Chamber, and as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014. She also co-founded Equality Now in 1992 alongside Jessica Neuwirth and Feryal Gharahi. The international women’s rights organisation works to advance women’s rights and challenge discriminatory laws and practices. The Norwegian Nobel Committee said the award recognised Pillay’s efforts to promote peace and international law, highlighting her role in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The committee described her as “a person who, with exceptional courage and integrity, has led the way towards a more comprehensive legal order”. It said she had been instrumental in ensuring that “war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted”. It also praised her commitment to universal legal principles and said she had helped hold states and national leaders accountable while bringing hope to victims of violence and conflict. “Peace requires justice,” the committee said, arguing that a legal system in which war criminals are held accountable and victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa congratulated Pillay on behalf of the nation, describing the award as a tribute to her courage, integrity and lifelong commitment to justice. “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally,” Ramaphosa said in a statement issued by his office. He said she had “served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can and should be a better place”. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also congratulated Pillay, praising her lifelong commitment to justice, peace and human dignity in a post on X. “Few have devoted their lives to justice, peace and human dignity like she did,” von der Leyen said. “From the violence of apartheid in South Africa to the horrors of the Rwandan genocide, she has confronted some of humanity’s darkest chapters. She has looked the brutality of injustice in the eye and never looked away.” The Nobel Peace Prize was first awarded in 1901. The 2026 award marks its 125th anniversary.

stories.headline: ECI’s credibility damaged, Gyanesh Kumar must resign: National Conference
stories.title: ECI’s credibility damaged, Gyanesh Kumar must resign: National Conference
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 9: The Jammu and Kashmir National Conference Friday strongly condemned the reported detentions of young people across the country ahead of INDIA block, CJP protest in Delhi against the Election Commission of India in New Delhi, police announcements in mosques asking people not to participate in the protest, cancellation of train services and measures to turn the national capital into a security forces cantonment. The party, as per a statement issued, described these actions as contrary to democratic principles and the Constitution. The party's Additional General Secretary and Rajya Sabha MP Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan said that the reality behind the BJP's repeated electoral victories had now come to light before the people of the country. He said that 9.7 million voters were excluded from the electoral rolls in West Bengal ahead of the elections, which contributed to the defeat of Mamata Banerjee's party, despite pre-election surveys and analyses indicating a likely victory for the Trinamool Congress. Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan said that the Election Commission had removed the names of 170 million voters across the country over the past several years, representing approximately 15 percent of the country's population. He said the Commission was duty-bound to ensure that every eligible citizen who had attained the age of 18 was registered as a voter. However the Commission was acting contrary to this responsibility by deleting people's names from the electoral rolls, a development he described as deeply unfortunate, alarming and a serious blow to democracy. He said recent revelations concerning the Election Commission of India had raised serious questions about the institution's credibility and that the matter was now also under consideration before the Supreme Court. Referring to the Supreme Court's observations, Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan said the Court had stated that it had no information regarding the permission for Form 6. He termed the matter serious, adding that falsely invoking the Supreme Court's permission to benefit a particular political party was an issue of grave concern. He said the circumstances demanded that the Chief Election Commissioner resign from office, arguing that the credibility of an institution entrusted with safeguarding the sanctity of democracy had been severely undermined. Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan strongly condemned the reported detentions across the country aimed at thwarting the protest scheduled by the CJP in New Delhi on October 10. He also criticised the alleged intimidation of Muslims to prevent them from participating in the protest, the suspension of railway services, the closure of metro stations and measures to turn the national capital into a military cantonment. He said the Constitution of India guaranteed every citizen the right to peaceful protest. However those in power were resorting to unconstitutional and undemocratic methods in an attempt to conceal their wrongdoings. Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan also strongly condemned the police restrictions imposed in recent days on protests by opposition Members of Parliament and prominent leaders. He said that if elected representatives of the people were being subjected to such treatment, the plight of ordinary citizens could only be imagined.

stories.headline: Acharya Vasugupta: The Sage Who Gave Kashmir Shaivism Its First Voice
stories.title: Acharya Vasugupta: The Sage Who Gave Kashmir Shaivism Its First Voice
stories.summary: Every great civilisation has moments when an idea becomes larger than the age in which it is born. In the intellectual history of Kashmir, Acharya Vasugupta represents one such moment. More than a millennium ago, he articulated a vision that became the starting point for one of India’s most sophisticated philosophical traditions—Kashmir Shaivism. Yet Vasugupta’s importance deserves to be understood precisely. He was not the author of the entire philosophical system that later came to be known as Kashmir Shaivism. The elaborate doctrines of the 36 tattvas, Pratyabhijna, Spanda, the various upayas and the aesthetic philosophy associated with Abhinavagupta emerged through generations of thinkers. Vasugupta’s distinctive place lies earlier: he stands at the foundational moment when the central Shaiva insight was expressed as a direct path of recognition and spiritual practice. His name is inseparably associated with the Shiva Sutras, a compact collection of aphorisms that opened a new chapter in Kashmiri thought. In remarkably few words, the text addresses questions that remain fundamental: Who are we? Why do we experience ourselves as limited? What is the relationship between the individual and the universe? And how can that limitation be overcome? The answers were not presented simply as doctrines to be believed. They were framed as invitations to experience. Vasugupta’s precise dates remain uncertain, and the accounts of his life combine history with sacred tradition. He is generally placed around the late eighth or early ninth century CE. Kashmir’s traditional accounts remember him as the sage to whom the Shiva Sutras were revealed. According to one celebrated tradition, Lord Shiva appeared to Vasugupta in a dream and directed him towards a rock on Mount Mahadeva, where the sacred teachings were revealed. Another account holds that the aphorisms were inscribed upon the rock itself and discovered by the sage. Whether understood literally or symbolically, the story expresses the extraordinary status attributed to the text. The Shiva Sutras were regarded not simply as the product of philosophical speculation but as a revelation of a truth that could be directly realised. What Vasugupta Actually Gave the Tradition The most important contribution associated with Vasugupta is the form in which the teaching was transmitted. The Shiva Sutras are not a systematic philosophical treatise. They do not proceed through long arguments or attempt to define every element of a complete metaphysical system. Instead, they offer terse propositions designed to provoke recognition. Their opening declaration is famous: “Chaitanyam Atma” — Consciousness is the Self. The significance of the statement lies not merely in the doctrine it expresses but in the direction it gives to spiritual inquiry. The seeker is asked to begin with the most immediate fact available: the experience of being aware. For Vasugupta, the search for the ultimate does not have to begin somewhere outside the individual. It begins with examining the very nature of the Self. This gives his teaching an important experiential quality. The individual ordinarily identifies the Self with the body, personality, memories, desires and circumstances. Vasugupta’s teaching turns that assumption around. These are changing aspects of experience; the deeper Self is that through which experience is known. The spiritual task is therefore not the acquisition of a new identity but the recognition of an identity that has been obscured by limitation. This is the distinctive seed that later thinkers would develop into the philosophy of Pratyabhijna, or recognition. Vasugupta did not, however, provide the elaborate philosophical formulation later associated with Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta. His contribution was more foundational and direct: he placed recognition at the heart of spiritual practice. That distinction matters. From Revelation to Practice Another distinctive feature of the Shiva Sutras is their practical orientation. The text moves repeatedly from metaphysical insight towards transformation. It deals with meditation, mantra, breath, concentration, perception and states of awareness. Its concern is not simply to explain reality but to show how a seeker might break through the ordinary limitations of experience. This makes Vasugupta different from a philosopher who merely constructs an abstract system. His teaching asks the reader to test the proposition within experience. If the Self is fundamentally free, why do we experience bondage? If the divine is present in all existence, why do we experience separation? If the deepest reality is present here and now, what prevents us from recognising it? These questions are implicit in the structure of the Shiva Sutras. The answer lies in limitation. Human beings habitually identify themselves with a contracted sense of individuality. Kashmir Shaiva thought would later analyse these limitations with considerable technical sophistication, but Vasugupta’s contribution was to establish the spiritual problem in experiential terms. The problem is not that the divine has disappeared. It is that recognition has been obscured. That is a crucial distinction. Liberation therefore becomes less a journey towards a distant goal and more a recovery of what is already present. The Early Vision of Spanda Vasugupta’s name is also closely connected by tradition with the early Spanda teaching. Spanda is frequently translated as “vibration,” although the term should not be confused with a physical vibration. It points towards the subtle dynamism or pulsation of ultimate reality—the fact that the supreme principle is not a lifeless abstraction but possesses the inherent power to manifest, perceive and act. This provided an important bridge between transcendence and the world. If Shiva is ultimate reality and Shakti is the power of manifestation, then creation is not something fundamentally outside the divine. The changing universe is related to the unchanging source through this dynamic power. The Spanda Karikas, traditionally connected with Vasugupta’s lineage, developed this insight. The exact historical relationship between Vasugupta and the text remains a matter of scholarly discussion, and it is therefore safer to speak of the Spanda tradition as belonging to the intellectual circle and lineage associated with him. What matters philosophically is that this early teaching prevented the Kashmir Shaiva vision from becoming a static doctrine of transcendence. Reality is dynamic. The divine is not merely beyond the world; it expresses itself through the world. This would become one of the most fertile ideas in the later development of Kashmir Shaivism. The Foundation and the Edifice After Vasugupta, the tradition expanded dramatically. Somānanda composed the Shivadristi. His disciple Utpaladeva developed the Ishvara Pratyabhijna, giving philosophical precision to the doctrine of recognition. Centuries later, Abhinavagupta brought together multiple streams of Kashmir Shaiva thought and produced a synthesis of extraordinary scope. It is tempting, therefore, to attribute the whole architecture of Kashmir Shaivism to Vasugupta. That would obscure his actual achievement. Vasugupta laid the foundation; the later masters built the philosophical edifice. His achievement was to establish a vocabulary and spiritual orientation from which subsequent generations could work. The Shiva Sutras supplied the compressed foundational insight. The Spanda tradition explored the dynamism of that insight. Later philosophers supplied increasingly elaborate metaphysics, logic and theology. Seen this way, Vasugupta’s importance becomes clearer, not smaller. He was the point at which a powerful spiritual intuition became a transmissible philosophical tradition. Why That Contribution Matters Today This distinction also makes Vasugupta more relevant to the present. The modern world is filled with elaborate systems for describing reality. Science, technology, psychology, economics and artificial intelligence constantly expand our capacity to measure and manipulate the external world. Vasugupta begins somewhere more elementary. He asks us to examine the experiencing subject itself. That question has acquired new urgency. Modern life is increasingly organised around the construction of identity. Professional profiles, social-media personas, biometric data, online reputations and algorithmic recommendations all contribute to the ways in which individuals are represented and understood. Yet none of these representations necessarily answers the simplest question: who is the person behind them? The Shiva Sutras approach this problem from an entirely different direction. Instead of adding another description of the self, they ask us to investigate the basis of selfhood. That is a distinctive contemporary relevance. The second concerns attention. Our age has developed an extraordinary machinery for capturing attention. Notifications, feeds, advertising and recommendation systems continually compete for a person’s mental space. opening: Every great civilisation has moments when an idea becomes larger than the age in which it is born.
In the intellectual history of Kashmir, Acharya Vasugupta represents one such moment.
body: More than a millennium ago, he articulated a vision that became the starting point for one of India’s most sophisticated philosophical traditions—Kashmir Shaivism.
Yet Vasugupta’s importance deserves to be understood precisely.
He was not the author of the entire philosophical system that later came to be known as Kashmir Shaivism.
The elaborate doctrines of the 36 tattvas, Pratyabhijna, Spanda, the various upayas and the aesthetic philosophy associated with Abhinavagupta emerged through generations of thinkers.
Vasugupta’s distinctive place lies earlier: he stands at the foundational moment when the central Shaiva insight was expressed as a direct path of recognition and spiritual practice.
His name is inseparably associated with the Shiva Sutras, a compact collection of aphorisms that opened a new chapter in Kashmiri thought.
In remarkably few words, the text addresses questions that remain fundamental: Who are we?
Why do we experience ourselves as limited?
What is the relationship between the individual and the universe?
And how can that limitation be overcome?
The answers were not presented simply as doctrines to be believed.
They were framed as invitations to experience.
Vasugupta’s precise dates remain uncertain, and the accounts of his life combine history with sacred tradition.
He is generally placed around the late eighth or early ninth century CE.
Kashmir’s traditional accounts remember him as the sage to whom the Shiva Sutras were revealed.
According to one celebrated tradition, Lord Shiva appeared to Vasugupta in a dream and directed him towards a rock on Mount Mahadeva, where the sacred teachings were revealed.
Another account holds that the aphorisms were inscribed upon the rock itself and discovered by the sage.
Whether understood literally or symbolically, the story expresses the extraordinary status attributed to the text.
The Shiva Sutras were regarded not simply as the product of philosophical speculation but as a revelation of a truth that could be directly realised.
What Vasugupta Actually Gave the Tradition.
The most important contribution associated with Vasugupta is the form in which the teaching was transmitted.
The Shiva Sutras are not a systematic philosophical treatise.
They do not proceed through long arguments or attempt to define every element of a complete metaphysical system.
Instead, they offer terse propositions designed to provoke recognition.
Their opening declaration is famous: “Chaitanyam Atma” — Consciousness is the Self.
The significance of the statement lies not merely in the doctrine it expresses but in the direction it gives to spiritual inquiry.
The seeker is asked to begin with the most immediate fact available: the experience of being aware.
For Vasugupta, the search for the ultimate does not have to begin somewhere outside the individual.
It begins with examining the very nature of the Self.
This gives his teaching an important experiential quality.
The individual ordinarily identifies the Self with the body, personality, memories, desires and circumstances.
Vasugupta’s teaching turns that assumption around.
These are changing aspects of experience; the deeper Self is that through which experience is known.
The spiritual task is therefore not the acquisition of a new identity but the recognition of an identity that has been obscured by limitation.
This is the distinctive seed that later thinkers would develop into the philosophy of Pratyabhijna, or recognition.
Vasugupta did not, however, provide the elaborate philosophical formulation later associated with Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta.
His contribution was more foundational and direct: he placed recognition at the heart of spiritual practice.
That distinction matters.
From Revelation to Practice Another distinctive feature of the Shiva Sutras is their practical orientation.
The text moves repeatedly from metaphysical insight towards transformation.
It deals with meditation, mantra, breath, concentration, perception and states of awareness.
Its concern is not simply to explain reality but to show how a seeker might break through the ordinary limitations of experience.
This makes Vasugupta different from a philosopher who merely constructs an abstract system.
His teaching asks the reader to test the proposition within experience.
If the Self is fundamentally free, why do we experience bondage?
If the divine is present in all existence, why do we experience separation?
If the deepest reality is present here and now, what prevents us from recognising it?
These questions are implicit in the structure of the Shiva Sutras.
The answer lies in limitation.
Human beings habitually identify themselves with a contracted sense of individuality.
Kashmir Shaiva thought would later analyse these limitations with considerable technical sophistication, but Vasugupta’s contribution was to establish the spiritual problem in experiential terms.
The problem is not that the divine has disappeared.
It is that recognition has been obscured.
That is a crucial distinction.
Liberation therefore becomes less a journey towards a distant goal and more a recovery of what is already present.
The Early Vision of Spanda Vasugupta’s name is also closely connected by tradition with the early Spanda teaching.
Spanda is frequently translated as “vibration,” although the term should not be confused with a physical vibration.

It points towards the subtle dynamism or pulsation of ultimate reality—the fact that the supreme principle is not a lifeless abstraction but possesses the inherent power to manifest, perceive and act.
This provided an important bridge between transcendence and the world.
If Shiva is ultimate reality and Shakti is the power of manifestation, then creation is not something fundamentally outside the divine.
The changing universe is related to the unchanging source through this dynamic power.
The Spanda Karikas, traditionally connected with Vasugupta’s lineage, developed this insight.

The exact historical relationship between Vasugupta and the text remains a matter of scholarly discussion, and it is therefore safer to speak of the Spanda tradition as belonging to the intellectual circle and lineage associated with him.
What matters philosophically is that this early teaching prevented the Kashmir Shaiva vision from becoming a static doctrine of transcendence.
Reality is dynamic.
The divine is not merely beyond the world; it expresses itself through the world.
This would become one of the most fertile ideas in the later development of Kashmir Shaivism.
The Foundation and the Edifice.
After Vasugupta, the tradition expanded dramatically.
Somānanda composed the Shivadristi.
His disciple Utpaladeva developed the Ishvara Pratyabhijna, giving philosophical precision to the doctrine of recognition.
Centuries later, Abhinavagupta brought together multiple streams of Kashmir Shaiva thought and produced a synthesis of extraordinary scope.
It is tempting, therefore, to attribute the whole architecture of Kashmir Shaivism to Vasugupta.
That would obscure his actual achievement.
Vasugupta laid the foundation; the later masters built the philosophical edifice.
His achievement was to establish a vocabulary and spiritual orientation from which subsequent generations could work.
The Shiva Sutras supplied the compressed foundational insight.
The Spanda tradition explored the dynamism of that insight.
Later philosophers supplied increasingly elaborate metaphysics, logic and theology.
Seen this way, Vasugupta’s importance becomes clearer, not smaller.
He was the point at which a powerful spiritual intuition became a transmissible philosophical tradition.
Why That Contribution Matters Today.
This distinction also makes Vasugupta more relevant to the present.
The modern world is filled with elaborate systems for describing reality.
Science, technology, psychology, economics and artificial intelligence constantly expand our capacity to measure and manipulate the external world.
Vasugupta begins somewhere more elementary.
He asks us to examine the experiencing subject itself.
That question has acquired new urgency.
Modern life is increasingly organised around the construction of identity.
Professional profiles, social-media personas, biometric data, online reputations and algorithmic recommendations all contribute to the ways in which individuals are represented and understood.
Yet none of these representations necessarily answers the simplest question: who is the person behind them?
The Shiva Sutras approach this problem from an entirely different direction.
Instead of adding another description of the self, they ask us to investigate the basis of selfhood.
That is a distinctive contemporary relevance.
The second concerns attention.
Our age has developed an extraordinary machinery for capturing attention.
Notifications, feeds, advertising and recommendation systems continually compete for a person’s mental space.
The issue is no longer simply having too much information; it is retaining the ability to determine where one’s attention goes.
Vasugupta’s insistence on disciplined awareness therefore acquires a new significance.
His teaching can be read as a reminder that attention is not merely an economic commodity; it is an element of freedom.
A person who cannot direct attention freely is vulnerable to every external demand.
A person who can observe thought without immediately becoming captive to it has begun to recover a degree of inner autonomy.
This is not a claim that Vasugupta anticipated the digital age.
He could not have.
His relevance is that he identified a human problem that technology has intensified without creating: the tendency to lose ourselves in the movements of the mind.
There is also a deeper contemporary challenge.
Humanity now possesses unprecedented technological power.
Artificial intelligence, biotechnology, digital networks and automation are transforming what human beings can do.
But increased capability raises a corresponding question: what kind of person should possess that capability?
Vasugupta’s philosophy does not provide a technological policy manual.
It offers something more fundamental—the insistence that outer power and inner understanding are not the same thing.
A civilisation may become increasingly powerful without becoming increasingly wise.
That distinction may be one of the most important reasons to revisit India’s philosophical inheritance today.
A Beginning, Not a Conclusion Vasugupta’s legacy should therefore not be measured only by the doctrines that later came to bear the name of Kashmir Shaivism.
His more distinctive contribution was to establish the first great doorway into that tradition.
He took an ultimate philosophical question and turned it into a question of immediate experience.
He presented the Self not as an object to be discovered somewhere beyond life, but as the starting point of inquiry.
He connected metaphysical insight with spiritual practice.
And through the Shiva Sutras, he provided later generations with a remarkably compressed set of teachings from which an entire philosophical world could unfold.
Somānanda, Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta would deepen, systematise and expand that world.
They would develop its logic, metaphysics, theology, aesthetics and psychology.
But the foundational gesture remained Vasugupta’s.
More than a thousand years later, its force has not disappeared.

At a time when people are surrounded by competing definitions of who they are, when attention has become a commodity and when technological power is advancing faster than reflection about its consequences, Vasugupta’s question is strikingly direct: Before we attempt to master the world, have we understood the one who experiences it?
That question takes us back to the opening of the Shiva Sutras and to the sage at the beginning of the Kashmiri tradition.
Vasugupta did not provide the final word on Kashmir Shaivism.
He did something perhaps more consequential.
He opened the first door.
(The Author is a columnist, a public intellectual and a noted legal eagle).

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (October 9, 2026) declined to intervene in the Tamil Nadu Assembly Speaker’s decision to close disqualification proceedings against a group of All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) legislators who had supported C. Joseph Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)-led government during the trust vote in May.
The court observed that the Speaker’s decision could not be challenged by an “interloper”.

A Bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana dismissed a plea filed by advocate P.V. Selvakumar, while observing that the sanctity of the constitutional mandate under the Tenth Schedule, which contains the anti-defection law, must be preserved.
“We are fully with you that sanctity of constitutional mandate must be preserved.
But we must understand workings of a democratic system,” the Bench said.

Mr. Selvakumar approached the Supreme Court after the Madras High Court rejected his petition challenging the Speaker’s June 9 decision to drop the disqualification proceedings against the AIADMK legislators.
The Speaker had acted on a May 27 letter from the party’s general secretary seeking withdrawal of the proceedings.
The High Court had held that Mr. Selvakumar, being a third party to the dispute, had no locus standi to interfere in the internal affairs of the AIADMK.
Advocate Nina Nariman, appearing for Mr. Selvakumar, argued that once the Speaker had entertained the disqualification petition, the proceedings ought to have been taken to their logical conclusion.
The legislators, she submitted, had defied the party whip by supporting the government in the confidence vote.
The Bench, however, drew a distinction between defection and differences that may arise within a political party in a multi-party democracy.
